edges.note: Baudouin de Courtenay's work is foundational for modern phonology (enwiki 'Jan Baudouin de Courtenay', oldid 1365158762: 'His work had a major influence on 20th-century linguistic theory, and it served as a foundation for several schools of phonology' and 'Three major schools of 20th-century phonology arose directly from his distinction between physiophonetic (phonological) and psychophonetic (morphophonological) alternations: the Leningrad school of phonology, the Moscow school of phonology, and the Prague school of phonology'; enwiki 'Phonology', oldid 1347090635, history section: "Baudouin de Courtenay's subsequent work, though often unacknowledged, is considered to be the starting point of modern phonology"). Britannica corroborates at the structural-linguistics grain ('regarded language sounds as structural entities, rather than mere physical phenomena, and thus anticipated the modern linguistic concern with language structure') but its body prose never names phonology — recorded against, not hidden. Whewell guard applied: the term 'phoneme' was coined in 1873 by A. Dufriche-Desgenettes, not by Baudouin, who (with Kruszewski and Shcherba) shaped its modern usage — this blocks any founding reading and does not touch 'influenced'. The morphophonology target was REJECTED in endpoint-closure-wave13-v1 (enwiki Morphophonology mentions him zero times) and is not re-proposed. Identity Q335092 verified live (P31=Q5, P570 1929-11-03; the item carries a second P569 claim 1846-03-13 — both encyclopedias state 13 March 1845, a minor item defect, not an identity problem; homonym Q11717009 'Polish journalist' ruled out). a-relation ladder (decision (68)): both endpoints reviewed + supported -> auto-reviewed.

Hooke discovered and named the cell (Micrographia, 1665), beginning the scientific study of cells (enwiki 'Cell (biology)', oldid 1367527367: 'Cells were discovered by Robert Hooke in 1665, who named them after their resemblance to cells in a monastery'; enwiki 'Cell theory', oldid 1365081375: 'This discovery is largely attributed to Robert Hooke, and began the scientific study of cells, known as cell biology'; Britannica 'Robert Hooke': 'first used the word cell to name the microscopic honeycomb cavities in cork, thereby contributing to the history of cell theory'). The FOUNDING reading was refuted at verification and is not claimed: term-coinage/observation is not founding (the Whewell rule), cell theory itself was formulated 1838-39 by Schleiden and Schwann (their reviewed founded_or_formalized edges carry that credit; record-not-resolve, this edge is additive at the influence grade, not competing), and enwiki records Hooke 'did not know their real structure or function' — 'What Hooke had thought were cells, were actually empty cell walls of plant tissues'. A microbiology-grain edge was considered and declined: Britannica's Leeuwenhoek and microbiology articles mention Hooke zero times (grep over full archived HTML), and enwiki notes Kircher (1658) as likely earlier observer of microbes; enwiki Robert Hooke does record 'the earliest-recorded observation of a microorganism, the microfungus Mucor' — recorded here, not promoted.
